slides.title: Chapter Route
slides.notes: Open by framing intersection as a classification problem rather than a yes-or-no test. The chapter moves from lines and segments to curves, convex polygons, and moving objects, but the same programming discipline keeps returning: represent the domain, compute candidates, reject impossible cases, and report enough contact information to debug a renderer or collision system.

slides.title: Intersection Contract
slides.notes: Use the contract slide to give students a reusable template for the rest of the lecture. A robust routine separates candidate generation from acceptance. The candidate might come from a two-by-two linear solve, a polynomial root, or a projection interval. The certificate then says why that candidate belongs to the geometric objects actually requested.

slides.title: Linear Components
slides.notes: Derive the determinant as the two-dimensional cross product that measures signed area. When it is safely nonzero, the carrier lines have one candidate point and the remaining work is parameter-domain filtering. When it is small, the routine changes character: it must distinguish parallel disjoint carriers from a shared carrier where interval overlap is the answer.

slides.title: Segment Return Types
slides.notes: Treat the segment slide as the first example of returning a geometric set. Students often write a segment intersection predicate and stop, but the chapter's pattern is richer. A point result and an interval result have different downstream behavior in clipping, collision response, and mesh repair, so the return type is part of the specification.

slides.title: Polyline And Polygon
slides.notes: Use this slide to prevent a common edge-loop bug. Intersecting a line or ray with polygon edges can be sufficient for many boundary queries, but a solid polygon changes the specification. A segment may lie entirely inside the polygon, so no edge reports a hit. Endpoint containment closes that hole before any acceleration structure is considered.

slides.title: Line Meets Curve
slides.notes: The curve slide shifts the audience from determinants to root finding. The same line can intersect the carrier curve twice while the requested segment contributes only one valid point. That distinction is exactly why the notebook checks residuals after drawing the figure: a root is useful only when it satisfies both the equation and the parameter domain.

slides.title: Curve-Curve Methods
slides.notes: For curve-curve intersections, emphasize that the chapter is not asking students to worship one method. Algebraic elimination gives exact-looking candidates but still needs residual checks. Polyline and bounding approaches trade symbolic compactness for spatial pruning. Raster-style methods can be appropriate for visualization, provided the result is understood as a sampled certificate rather than exact geometry.

slides.title: Separating Axes
slides.notes: The separating-axis slide is the chapter's central compression trick for convex objects. Instead of searching for crossing edges first, project both polygons onto a candidate normal and ask whether the one-dimensional intervals overlap. If one axis has a gap, that axis is a certificate of nonintersection. If no candidate axis separates them, convexity supplies the positive answer.

slides.title: Moving Polygons
slides.notes: The moving version is a clean example of why static predicates are not enough in collision detection. For each axis, a gap may close or widen according to relative speed. The algorithm preserves a global interval of times that have survived every axis so far. First contact is the latest entrance, not the first axis examined.

slides.title: Contact Set
slides.notes: This is where the algorithm becomes useful for contact response. A Boolean collision time tells when something happened, but not what touched. By saving whether projection extrema were vertices or edges on the critical axis, the routine can construct a point or segment contact set. That feature pair is the bridge to impulse, clipping, or manifold generation.

slides.title: Degeneracy Clinic
slides.notes: Slow down on this slide because numerical ambiguity is not an implementation detail to hide at the end. A tolerance rule encodes a geometric convention. Relative determinant tests, explicit endpoint policies, and residual checks make the convention inspectable. The goal is not to remove degeneracy; it is to make the reported result reproducible and explainable.

slides.title: Implementation Lab
slides.notes: Close by turning the lecture back into a reproducible notebook workflow. The chapter's visuals are not decoration; each one exists to inspect a branch of the algorithm. Ask students to keep the four sanity checks alive as they modify the data. That makes the exercise about geometric trust, not about copying an isolated formula.
